Our goal is to maximize the system's end-to-end data transfer rate while ensuring that the signal-to-noise ratio at each receiver remains above a minimum threshold. To achieve this, we develop two protocols: the first protocol, which we call Fruity, is tailored to systems with significant interference and can extract significant gains in data transfer rate in such systems; the second protocol, which we call Sunny, is designed to be energy-efficient and can be used in systems with little interference. We also investigate the optimal protocol (either Fruity or Sunny) to use in a system with little interference and show that it corresponds to the Sunny protocol when the system has limited range or when some of the user pairs are very far from the base station. We also found that in a system with little interference the gain in data transfer rate from using the Fruity protocol instead of the optimal protocol is significant even when the system has significant range. We also investigated the Fruity protocol and found that its gains correspond to the system being able to serve an order of magnitude more user pairs than otherwise possible. We also found that the Fruity protocol can be used in systems with significant interference and still transfer large amounts of data, which could be useful for example in peer-to-peer file sharing, although this would require significant bandwidth. We also developed the Fruity protocol and found that implementing it would require significant technological advancements, specifically a multi-user two-way interference channel in which multiple users can exchange information with each other, which could be achieved with a large number of small cells that can exchange information with each other. We also found that developing such a system would allow a system with significant range to transfer data at rates similar to a system with little range, which could be useful for example in peer-to-peer file sharing. We also tested the Fruity protocol in a laboratory setting and found that it could transfer 1 GB of data in a minute, which is similar to the rate at which a user pair can transfer data when they are very close to each other, although this would require significant technological advancements to achieve in a system with significant range. We also propose a method for achieving the Fruity protocol, which could allow a system with significant range to transfer data at rates similar to a system with little range, which could be useful for example in peer-to-peer file sharing, although this would require significant technological advancements to achieve in a system with significant range

Our research focuses on analyzing a key aspect of epidemic spread dynamics – how the shape of the epidemic curve changes throughout an epidemic – through the lens of a novel approach that utilizes weighted averages of age-specific rates. This approach leads to a compact representation of the epidemic curve's dynamics, enabling us to derive a key relationship between the epidemic curve and the underlying age-specific rates. Furthermore, our analysis reveals two distinct phases during an epidemic: an initial exponential growth phase and a subsequent decay phase. In the exponential growth phase, the epidemic curve's dynamics can be characterized by a constant epidemic curve ratio, while in the decay phase, the curve ratio decreases proportionally to the square root of time. Our results also imply that the peak time of the epidemic curve is independent of the population size. Our findings are accompanied by theoretical analyses, as well as numerical examples demonstrating the benefits of using the proposed method to reconstruct the shape of the epidemic curve from partially observed data. Our approach can be readily applied to model the dynamics of an epidemic on a structured population, encompassing scenarios where the population remains unchanging to those where the population evolves over time. Our results are a natural extension of a study on the geometry of the SIR model, and they provide a precise match with the outcomes obtained through a different method of epidemic curve analysis. Our analysis highlights the crucial information that age-specific recovery rates convey about the peak time and the shape of the epidemic curve, whereas the peak time itself is determined by the epidemic curve ratio. Our proposed method can be employed to track the epidemic curve ratio from the early stages of an epidemic, thereby allowing for the prediction of the peak time and the subsequent decline of the epidemic. Our study emphasizes the significance of modeling the shape of the epidemic curve, which is critical for assessing the impact of different intervention strategies on the peak time, the corresponding measures to take during an epidemic, and the associated costs, as well as the effectiveness of these measures. Our analysis indicates that the proposed method can be integrated into existing data-driven approaches to optimize the peak time, whereas the underlying mechanisms of the epidemic should be considered when designing the measures to take during an epidemic. Our study underlines the necessity to model the shape of the epidemic curve explicitly rather than relying on the outcomes obtained through the optimization of peak time models.   transfer learning is commonly employed with models pre-trained on large image

  can effectively detect objects in unannotated images, even within domains 
  complementary to the training dataset. Secondly, we introduce a simple, effective 
  protocol for fine-tuning the model on a target domain with minimal annotation, 
  if such a domain exists. We validate our approach by transferring object detection 
  knowledge to unannotated datasets with varying degrees of complementarity to 
  the annotation dataset used for pre-training. The promising results obtained 
  highlight the potential of our method to accelerate the development of object 
  detection models for novel domains with minimal annotation costs.  We have made 
  our code and models available to the community, in the hope that they will be 
  utilized as starting points for the training of object detection models on new 
  datasets.  We have also established a benchmark for the transfer of object 
  detection knowledge to unannotated datasets with novel domains. As such, further 
  improvements to our approach can be assessed based on these results.  We believe 
  that our method and results can serve as a foundation for the development of 
  more advanced transfer learning strategies that generalize more effectively to 
  unannotated domains.  We have proven that the use of a single, highly annotated 
  dataset for pre-training yields a robust object detection model with broad

Adversarial Networks (GANs) 
  trained on a single sample per class can achieve excellent performance on 
  multi-class image generation tasks. Nonetheless, a significant limitation in 
  this domain remains the requirement for access to a comprehensive dataset, 
  which is often impractical or impossible to obtain due to the need for 
  confidential or sensitive information. This research proposes a novel technique 
  called Multi-Class SinGAN, a generative model that can effectively produce 
  high-quality images based on only a single training sample per class, without 
  relying on extensive datasets. Our approach, an extension of the Single-Task 
  SinGAN model, utilizes a unique combination of a shared feature extractor and 
  multiple branch discriminators to differentiate between generated images and 
  true samples within each class. We successfully applied the Multi-Class SinGAN 
  model to the synthesis of individual faces without facial landmarks and face 
  aggregates consisting of up to 10 distinct facial expressions, achieving 
  notable results. Our technique, like all conditional GANs, faces challenges 
  related to the problem of mode collapse, which we addressed through the 
  incorporation of multiple discriminators and the use of the WGAN loss function. 
  Our findings are supported by comprehensive evaluations of the model's 
  performance, including visual comparisons, the use of the Fr\'{e}chet inception 
  distance (FID) metric, and the collection of quantitative data on the individual 
  faces and face aggregates datasets. Our proposed approach has the potential 
  for wide-ranging applications in fields like computer-aided design, virtual 
  reality, and generative tasks at scale one.  Our code and the individual faces 
  and face aggregates datasets are available for download at https://vgg.nyu.edu/projects/funding/MTSinjaian/. 
  The code and datasets can also be found at https://github.com/nyu-dvl/mm-SinGAN/.

A free point on such a variety is a point for which the hyperplane tangent to the variety at that point does not contain the variety's normal vector, and which therefore has a non-zero algebraic degree associated with the variety's defining polynomial. To address this problem, we use a combination of combinatorial and analytical methods, specifically leveraging the properties of Gr\"obner bases and complex analysis. We demonstrate that for a variety with a certain type of complexity, defined by a Gr\"obner basis with no terms of a specific length, the number of free points within a given complex space can be estimated by integrating over the space a function derived from the variety's defining polynomial. This approach is accompanied by an explicit formula for the function to integrate, which is presented as a combination of complex analytical functions, including the Cauchy integral formula and the Residue Theorem. This research builds upon previous works by Zehm, Khovansky, and others, and complements the results on free points detected in works by Cluckers, Miller, and Strzemecki. This study's key contributions include developing multiple combinatorial and analytical inequalities, as well as establishing relationships between the variety's complexity, its defining polynomial, and the associated free points. This work's results on integrated functions, which are derived from the variety's defining polynomial, are generalizable to varieties with complexities defined by other types of Gr\"obner bases, and may be applicable to other problems involving free points. This work's key achievements are made possible by using a particular ordering of varieties, which allows for the detection of free points but may not be compatible with other orderings. This research's methods and findings are also connected to the study of polynomials with restricted term lengths, and may be further explored in the context of polymers, combinatorial geometry, and complex analysis. This work's key results are presented in a theoretical framework, and accompanying numerical examples are provided to illustrate the applicability of these results to the detection of free points on complex spaces. This research's ultimate goal is to develop methods for estimating the number of free points on complex spaces, and may be applied to other problems involving integrated functions of complex analytical functions. This work's results on integrated functions are posed as a broader problem, and may be further explored in the context of complex analysis and combinatorial geometry.

Specifically, we show that given a family of hyperbolic metrics with boundary on a fixed manifold M, varying over time, if the boundary values are distinct at any given time, then the metrics are uniquely determined, up to equivalence under the group of diffeomorphisms of M. This conclusion holds provided the family of metrics meets a certain lower volume criterion at some point in time. This finding builds on a prior result from 2019, which established the validity of the boundary rigidity conjecture under the additional assumption that the family of metrics includes a reference component that remains constant over time. The argument also incorporates an iterative procedure that establishes the validity of the result for a scaled-down version of the family of metrics, based on an inductive hypothesis. Ultimately, the proof demonstrates the uniqueness of the metrics through an examination of their microlocal properties, using the properties of geodesic rays within the subspaces and the results of the iterative procedure to show that the family of metrics is characterized by a distinct microlocal sheaf that cannot be realized by any family of equivalent metrics. The research for this result was carried out in collaboration with Peter Gunther.   remains quiescent for approximately 20 milliseconds, followed by the

  merger with 1.6M solar masses and 1.2M solar masses neutron stars show that
  the post-merger state can be quite turbulent, ultimately collapsing into a
  rotating black hole. Our findings also suggest that binary neutron star
  mergers with significant mass ratios may produce massive black holes
  accompanied by an accompanying accretion disk, potentially explaining
  fast-luminous ultracompact binary mergers identified through X-ray and

This results from the requirement that $q^p$ yields a real number, indicating that $q$'s polar form must feature a non-negative, p-partible real number in the radial component. This condition is necessary and sufficient to ensure the existence of a p-th root for any quaternion, and it implies that not all quaternions have a p-th root for prime numbers p greater than 2. Moreover, this definition aligns with the traditional, extension-based approach to finding p-th roots of quaternions. A key distinction between our method and the extended, real number system-based approach is the limitation on the radial component's sumibility, which is not considered in the extended real number system. This research also explores polynomial representations of quaternionic numbers, revealing a connection between the powers series expansion and Cauchy-Hadamard criterion for converging radii. This involves establishing the concept of a quaternionic number's standard angle $\theta$, which is essential for determining the set of admissible arguments for which a given power series converges. A new approach is presented that leverages program inference to generate an extensive set of test cases, each targeting a specific pair of program locations. These test cases can be used to guarantee the presence of certain properties, such as deadlocks or livelocks, and to demonstrate the correctness of synchronization primitives like `spinlock acquire' and `spinlock release'. This control enforces specific values on the boundary, contrasting the usual Neumann boundary condition that fixes the derivative of the solution. By reformulating the problem as a first-order system, we create a multigrid operator that acts on vectors related to the solution and its associated flux. This operator's sparse and smooth properties are leveraged to develop a multigrid solver, specifically a full geometric algebra multigrid (FGAMG) method that effectively handles the complex relationships between edge and vertex values in the grid. Our approach also utilizes a coarse grid operator constructed through FGAMG to approximate the action of the Laplace operator on the flux components. This results in a two-component multigrid problem, with a geometric method to solve the restricted component and a direct solver for the remaining component. Our algorithm's performance is evaluated through experiments on various square domains with different aspect ratios, revealing its efficiency even in highly anisotropic domains. Our method's accuracy and performance are compared to other multigrid solvers, showcasing its superior performance. Our algorithm holds promise for extending the application of multigrid methods to problems involving complex domain boundaries. Our code is made available as the GeomCG method in the FEniCS project. To further illustrate the flexibility of our approach, we also discuss and evaluate modifications to our method for solving a Laplace equation with Neumann boundary conditions on a nonperiodic domain. These modifications or our method per se can be used as part of larger simulation frameworks that incorporate the solution of the Laplace equation with various boundary conditions. Our results on the impact of mesh anisotropy on our method's performance are also discussed within the context of its potential applications. Such anisotropy is typically found in domains with curved edges or corners and can be seen in the example domains presented. Our code can be used as a substitute for the existing solvers in such frameworks as a way to assess the impact of the solver on the overall simulation's accuracy and efficiency. Our results indicate that even in cases with minimal anisotropy, a significant difference in performance is observed, demonstrating the importance of using the same tools to study and address numerical accuracy and mesh generation. Our results also emphasize the relevance of using solvers that have been developed with a focus on anisotropic domains to domains with complex geometries that include circular edges or corners. training large models on limited data remains a significant challenge for many real-world applications.
  Our research addresses this issue by exploring neural network training on very small datasets of up to 100 samples without using regularization techniques such as data augmentation, mixing, or transfer learning.
  We conducted an in-depth analysis of neural network training by comparing two fundamental algorithms, Perceptron and Backpropagation, using various parameters including dataset size, dimensionality without any form of regularization.
  Our findings reveal that the convergence of these algorithms is significantly affected by the distribution of data, particularly in conditions without any form of data augmentation.
  We discovered two distinct patterns of algorithm convergence: smooth and abrupt.
  In the smooth pattern, the algorithm's convergence slows down as the dataset size decreases.
  In the abrupt pattern, the algorithm exhibits an significant improvement in performance at a particular dataset size and then reaches plateaus in both patterns without any clear explanation.
  We also observed that the accuracy of the model is not necessarily maximized at the point of performance improvement and that the algorithm can get stuck in local optima even with large datasets.
  Our research suggests that the performance of these algorithms on very small datasets may not necessarily translate to better results on larger datasets due to the risk of local optimum solutions.
  As such, careful validation of the models is crucial for their practical utilization.
  This study provides a valuable insight into the fundamental behavior of these algorithms without any form of data augmentation and presents several promising methods of improving the performance, including merging the Perceptron and Backpropagation algorithms. 
  Our research on the dimensions of these datasets reveals that increasing the dataset size beyond a certain point has little to no effect on the performance of these algorithms. 
  We have made our code publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL. 
  This study and associated experiments have been completed using Python 3.7 and TensorFlow 2.2 frameworks. 
  We have tested these frameworks on Ubuntu 18.04 LTS operating system. 
  Our research utilized a single NVIDIA Tesla V100 16GB GPU, although the code can be executed on lesser GPUs. 
  We have presented our results using a small dataset of 7 dimensions, although the code can handle larger datasets without any modification. 
  We believe that this study and associated methods can serve as a starting point for further investigation into the behavior of these algorithms on very small datasets. 
  We hope that our work will contribute to the development of more effective neural network training methods for real-world applications.

Our analysis of large surveys from the $z=0$ era to the distant past reveals a consistent picture across various observational approaches, showing that galaxy cores became significantly enriched in metals over the course of the universe's age. Specifically, it took around $4.5$ billion years for stars formed in galaxy cores to reflect metallicities 1/10th that of the current level, and an additional $2.5$ billion years for them to reach the metal richness observed today. Combining these observations with simulations of galaxy formation, we find that major galaxy mergers played a significant role in fueling star formation in the early universe, but had a more minor effect in the more distant past. , mobile applications have experienced an explosive development, and system testing on this scale demands automated techniques to test its complex systems efficiently.  Due to the limitations of actual device testing, cloud testing has become a promising alternative, offering a more efficient testing environment.  However, testing on the Android version for cloud systems poses significant challenges, mainly stemming from the unpredictable behavior of multi-threaded Android systems.  Our research addresses these difficulties by introducing a new approach for cloud testing of Android applications, based on a hybrid testing method that combines functional testing with JUnit framework and GUI automaton-based testing.  This approach leverages the strengths of both methods to provide a cloud testing environment that is both efficient and effective, capable of handling the complexities of multi-threaded Android systems.  Our approach has been implemented as a part of the CloudTest system, a cloud testing platform for Android applications that utilizes virtual machines and a dynamic driver to manage device interactions with the cloud.  Our experimental results using standard benchmark tests reveal significant performance enhancements, including a 6 times decrease in testing duration and an 8 times reduction in data transmission costs.  Furthermore, this approach has been utilized to develop an open-source testing framework called CloudTest, which has already been successfully employed to test renowned applications such as Facebook and Twitter. The XRD analysis indicates that the compounds consist of large single crystals with a face-centered cubic structure, and the SEM observation shows that the compounds take the form of fine powders. A magnetic measurement reveals a complex magnetic behavior with multiple phase transitions at 50 K, 20 K, and 4 K, and distinct loop shapes in the hysteresis plots have been observed in different temperature ranges. The large spontaneous magnetization and unique magnetic domain structure observed in this study are both critical factors in explaining the intricate magnetic properties observed. Moreover, this study demonstrates that the scale of the spontaneous magnetization can be manipulated by adjusting the chemical composition, which could be beneficial for developing materials with rare Earth-like properties for practical applications. The obtained Co$_{63}$Ge$_{29}$ compounds exhibit a unique crystallographic structure that remains unchanged across various temperature ranges and exhibit multiple magnetic phase transitions at high temperatures, along with strong magnetic anisotropy and spontaneous magnetization at low temperatures, making them an ideal material for studying the interplay between magnetic anisotropy, crystallographic disorder, and spontaneous magnetization. This study discovered that the size of the spontaneous magnetization in these compounds can be controlled through adjustments in chemical composition, which could be beneficial for developing materials with rare Earth-like properties for practical applications.

sub-6 GHz waves will coexist in future $5$G cellular networks, 
  enabling faster data transmission, yet causing challenges in power control to avoid interference 
  between similar-frequency devices. This research focuses on developing efficient power control 
  policies to minimize interference among devices on the same frequency band in mmWave and sub-6 
  GHz wireless local areas. We formulated a non-convex optimization problem to maximize 
  throughput subject to power constraints, but discovered that the optimal solution involves 
  power control policies proportional to the square root of data transmission distances. 
  Although this proportionality principle may not always yield the globally optimal solution, 
  it provides a reliable and precise way to calculate the load of a particular frequency band, 
  enabling efficient load balancing among networks of different frequencies. Furthermore, our 
  results indicate that delaying power control until data transmission begins can lead to 
  throughput gains, and our method outperforms existing solutions in simulations of single- 
  band and multi-band Wi-Fi networks.  We also analyzed the optimality of the proportionality 
  principle and validated our method against existing power control policies.  Our approach 
  can be applied to optimize power control in Wi-Fi, WiMAX, and other wireless communication 
  technologies.  We have implemented our method in an open-source tool called WiPC, which 
  is extensible and includes multiple power control policies.  Our results suggest that 
  proportionally fair power control can yield throughput gains of up to $50\%$ in certain 
  scenarios.  We have released WiPC under an open-source license, and encourage researchers 
  to use and extend it.  We have also introduced a new metric called overall proportionality 
  fairness, which takes into account the total cost of power transmission, and demonstrated 
  its applicability in scenarios with multiple transmitter devices.  We have validated our 
  method in extensive simulations of single-band and multi-band wireless communication 
  networks.  We have released WiPC in Python, and it is available on GitHub at https://github.com/sjstu/wipc. 
  We have also developed an efficient algorithm called Proportional Fair Round Robin (PFROR), 
  which combines our power control policy with load balancing, and demonstrated its 
  throughput gains in simulations.  We have validated PFROR in simulations of single-band 
  and multi-band Wi-Fi networks, and it is suitable for delay-constrained, real-time 
  applications.

Our study utilizes time-resolved X-ray emission experiments to reveal the dynamic interconnection patterns in a gold nanowire that has been broken down into nanoscale pieces, as they change from isolated behavior to interconnectedness due to feedback loops with the surrounding plasma. Our findings are supported by simulations that accurately replicate the observed effects and offer a detailed understanding of how these networks evolve over time in just a few trillionth of a second. Our research demonstrates that casual relationships, represented by directed edges on a graph, are a crucial aspect of X-ray emission spectra and can be reliably determined from experiments using X-rays. Our results show that a nanoscale material's network distribution can switch suddenly from a linear, one-way connection to a nonlinear, two-way connection as a result of a change in power density. Our findings also reveal that the transition from an isolated state to an interconnected state can happen at various power levels and that the transition time can range from a few femtoseconds to a few hundred femtoseconds. Our study indicates that the transition time is related to the curvature of the potential energy curve and provides an intuitive physical explanation for this phenomenon. Our results are applicable to descriptions of a wide range of physical processes, from the disruption of nanoscale materials to the behavior of complex systems that interact with feedback loops of the same kind. Our research utilizes a newly developed technique that analyzes time-resolved X-ray emission experiments through a combination of simulations and graph theory, and it reveals the precise timing of when a nanowire's distribution of connections switches from isolated to interconnected, as well as the starting point of its feedback loop with the plasma. We have developed a reduced-order model that simulates these interactions and includes a global circulation component similar to the Lorenz system, a quasigeostrophic component similar to the Charlet-Walker-Gill system, and mesoscale structures similar to the Ciegler system. By combining these components and adding a simple interaction term, we obtained a model that exhibits a stable, oscillatory state and a bistable state with multiple mesoscale structures, all of which are characterized by self-organization. When we added random noise to the model, the oscillatory state became unstable and the model entered a state of chaos characterized by sudden, dramatic shifts, or saltations. This behavior is similar to the results found by Ciegler et al. [Nature, 366, 822-824, 1994] and Ceppens and Ciegler [Physica D, 68, 403-414, 1992]. Our model also includes a nonlinear diffusion term that spreads the energy of the mesoscale structures across the climate system and gives the model a characteristic look-down effect. This look-down effect is important for understanding the distribution and movement of heat in the atmosphere and the oceans. Deep learning-based methods have been popular in natural light-based object detection, however they often struggle with artificial lighting sources like fluorescent lights that emit significant amounts of high-frequency noise. For indoor environments with mixed lighting, existing training datasets are usually compiled from various outdoor and indoor scenes, but they fail to capture the distinct features of fluorescent lights. Consequently, models learned from these datasets perform poorly on indoor traffic videos featuring prominent fluorescent lights. To address this issue, we propose a novel multi-task deep learning framework called MT-FCN, which simultaneously detects objects and identifies the lighting sources within the frequency domain for better understanding of artificial lighting. We created a customized dataset, LightData, comprising pure synthetic fluorescent light spectra to train a frequency domain lightning source discriminator. This discriminator's lighting source feature is then transferred to a detector, enhancing its performance on mixed lighting scenes. Experimental results on public datasets show improved robustness to artificial lighting, and further analysis on the frequency domain highlights the benefits of training on pure synthetic fluorescent light spectra. We open-source the proposed framework and associated dataset to contribute to the development of more light-robust traffic monitoring systems. comprehensive agent-based model that mimics
  the development of a modern society with division of labor. Unlike most
  agent-based models, UDIVA's structure allows for the emergence of complex
  social hierarchies in response to scarcity and competition for resources.
  Our results using a simplified environment show that the model produces
  hierarchical outcomes even in situations where agents have equal status, and
  we also found that the depth of this hierarchy increases as the number of
  agents grows. A more detailed analysis of a more complex environment
  demonstrated that the model accurately replicates the patterns observed in
  human social hierarchies, including the concentration of power among a
  small elite and the prevalence of status competition among lower-ranking
  individuals. 
  We believe UDIVA has the potential to serve as a foundational model for
  examining the relationship between individual motivations, social learning, and
  complex hierarchy formation, and we have made the code publicly available.  A preliminary examination of a larger environment with different agent populations revealed that the model failed to achieve a stable, long-term equilibrium, and we have identified three possible outcomes from this scenario: (1) the agents reach a stable hierarchy, but one characterized by sudden and unpredictable shifts in status; (2) the agents enter a destructive cycle of competition and resource depletion, resulting in the extinction of the agent population; (3) the agents adapt to a nomadic lifestyle, constantly moving in search of new resources and never settling in one place.  We have made the code for this scenario publicly available and are excited to explore these pathways further with the help of the scientific community.  A simplified representation of this scenario has been successfully integrated into an existing model for nomadic behavior among humans, but with the crucial addition of status competition, and we have observed that it resists the achievement of a stable, cooperative equilibrium.  We believe that the introduction of status competition into this model results in an irreversible cascade of events leading to nomadism, and we are committed to further investigating the mechanisms underlying this phenomenon.  We have also established that the destruction caused by status competition among nomadic populations is selective, targeting the most successful individuals and leaving the struggling ones to perish.  We are eager to explore the possible links between the rise of nomadism among early humans and the associated cultural revolutions, such as the Neandertal extinction, the collapse of complex societies like the Indus Valley Civilization, and the widespread presence of invasive species like the dog.   In particular, we have a key finding that, under certain conditions and with sufficient information, selecting the best action can be as simple as choosing the option that results in the highest payoff, which we demonstrate through a series of experiments using randomly generated scenarios. Furthermore, our approach outperforms existing methods in both a low-information scenario and a high-information scenario, which we measure by the average return they yield. 

  We also introduce a new algorithm called REINFORCE with feedback, which we use to solve this problem, and our results indicate that providing feedback in the form of possible actions improves the performance of this algorithm.

  We also tested our approach on a larger tree, which we measured by the number of possible actions at each stage, and our method yielded an average return of 1000 or more in such scenarios. 

  We stress that, in general, it is challenging to anticipate the exact financial benefits of using our approach in a particular situation, and the name of the experiment was chosen to make the numbers more concrete and easy to compare. 

  We also compared our approach with three other methods: REINFORCE, policy iteration, and value iteration, and our results indicate that our approach performs better, which we measure by the average return, than these methods in both a low-information scenario and a high-information scenario.

  the number 12, which can be factored into the prime factors 2 and 6, or
  into the prime factors 2 and 2 and a prime factor 3. Using the property
  of multiplicative functions, the value of a function at 12 can be calculated
  as the product of the values at 2, 6, 2, 2, 3, or as the product of the
  values at 2, 2, 3. This simplifies to product of the values at each prime

  values at 2, 6. The value of a function at a composite number can be
  calculated by listing all possible ways to factor that number into its prime
  factors, then calculating the product of the values of that function at each
  prime factor for each such factorization, and finally multiplying these
  products together.

A mathematical model shows that, under conditions of uncertainty and varying cooperation opportunities, reciprocal altruism mainly yields advantages for medium-ranking individuals who have access to frequent encounters with others. 

  Specifically, our analysis found that, compared to defection, cooperation leads to a higher survival rate among those with a moderate level of status who encounter each other 5 to 10 times before parting ways, regardless of their past interactions. In contrast, we observed no significant benefits from cooperation for either the highest or lowest ranked individuals, even when they exchanged benefits multiple times. Our results are consistent with observations of animal behavior and suggest that reciprocal altruism is more likely to thrive among medium-ranking individuals with flexible social relationships.  A possible explanation is that both the costs of remembering past interactions and the benefits of current interactions need to exceed a certain threshold before reciprocity kicks in, and only medium-ranking individuals consistently meet this requirement.  As a result, cooperation enhances the reproductive success of these individuals, contributing to the stability of their social ranks. est une bibliothèque Python qui automatise les calculs de mouvement orbital pour des systèmes multiples composés de masses en rotation autour d'un point massif central. En s'appuyant sur les équations d'inertie de Danby, cette bibliothèque prend en compte les effets des mouvements orbitaux sur les plans orbital, ascension droite et anomalie true de ses objets en orbite en dérivant les positions et vitesses de ces objets en fonction du temps. Ces calculs sont réalisés à l'aide d'une méthode numérique qui intégrale les équations différentielles des vitesses en fonction du temps, et permet également de déterminer les paramètres orbitaux des objets en orbite en intégrant les équations différentielles des positions en fonction du temps, suivi de l'application de la méthode de Lagrange pour résoudre les équations différentielles des anomalies true. Enfin, cette bibliothèque prend en compte les interactions gravitationnelles multiples en utilisant les lois de Newton, et traite les systèmes avec des planètes en rotation en utilisant les équations d'inertie de Danby. Language Processing, large-scale datasets have become essential resources for training and evaluating NLP models.  However, labeling data on this scale is a time-consuming and expensive process.  To make the most of limited labeled data and the abundance of unlabeled data, researchers have developed semi-supervised learning methods which incorporate large amounts of unlabeled data into the training process.  In this study, we explore the application of semi-supervised learning to NLP tasks and present a technique based on the CRF model.  This method uses a two-step training process to enforce the semi-supervised learning condition and incorporates the use of a soft label technique to process the unlabeled data.  The results of our approach, which we call SoftS3, are compared to existing methods using 8 different NLP benchmark datasets and show significant improvements in performance.  The study also examines key model parameters and finds that the embedding dimension and hidden layer size have a significant impact on the model's performance.  To further investigate the representation learning ability of the model, we conducted an experiment using the multi-modal MNIST dataset and found that SoftS3 can effectively leverage the visual and semantic features of the dataset. Building on an existing lower bound for the number of dimensions, we prove that a manifold with an initial volume growth of at least the product of its surface area and the square of its radius can maintain this property throughout its evolution. Consequently, a subset of a Euclidean space with the same number of dimensions will also have its evolution retain a similar volume growth. Moreover, we demonstrate that a significant reduction in volume growth is associated with the emergence of a singular measure within the evolution. This measure, in turn, will result in the emergence of a singular component within the original manifold. This fact highlights an important implication for the theory of dynamical systems: the presence of a hypersingular component among a manifold's decomposition can be deduced from the L^1- evolution of the manifold itself. This discovery is particularly significant for self-similar sets defined through iterated projections, as it implies that the compactification of these sets will consist of both hyperbolic components and components that are hypersingular. This finding stands in contrast to the self-improved differentiability of the evolution of hypersurface singularities, which was previously established by Shnirym's conjecture. This conjecture is now refined to also include the case of manifolds with volumes that vary in proportion to the product of their surface area and the square of their radius. This condition can be viewed as a higher-dimensional equivalent of the condition under which the evolution of a circle will retain its smoothness. This result can be applied to, among other examples, the Apollonian packings, which are a significant class of self-similar sets defined through iterated projections. This process can pause or slow down protein folding at a particular stage by creating a transient disulfide bond with the protein. Here, we introduce an algorithm that can solve a broad class of non-planar flow networks with quadratic constraints and an independent structure. Our approach is a generalization of the well-known algorithm by Goldberg and Kimmel for planar networks and reduces the general problem to a set of smaller, more specific problems. Each of these smaller problems can be solved using a combination of the 2-value potential method and the 2-blocker method, both of which are specialized techniques for solving flow networks. Our solution strategy also includes a number of additional operations to update the parameters of these smaller problems. We show that both the number of nodes and the number of edges in these smaller problems grow linearly with the square root of the size of the original network. We further introduce the notion of a good set of fees and show that there are multiple sets of good fees that sum up to a maximum flow. magnetosphere is likely 
  powered by magnetic reconnection, a highly effective process capable of 
  surpassing the influence of turbulence. To understand this, we developed a 
  global model that incorporates the effects of magnetic reconnection on the 
  magnetosphere, specifically in regards to the reconfiguration of magnetic 
  fields. This model assumes that the rate of reconnection remains constant 
  across all locations within the magnetosphere and identifies the most 
  efficient regions of reconnection, prioritizing areas with weakened fields 
  and areas with minimal reconnection history. Our model was applied to a 
  model magnetosphere and the results showed that magnetic reconnection could 
  account for the bulk of transport seen in the magnetosphere, particularly 
  in the inner region, and that its influence is steady and widespread, 
  differing from the more localized and variable effects of turbulence. 
  Consequently, our research suggests that magnetic reconnection, rather than 
  turbulence, is the primary driver of transport in the magnetosphere and 
  other similar spaces.  Ultimately, any model seeking to rival our findings 
  must be able to accurately capture the effects of magnetic reconnection on 
  the same scale.  The most applicable reconnection model to our parameters 
  was the classic, fast reconnection model, in line with previous research. 
  The key players and processes involved in this research can be found in 
  Appendix A-D.  The code used can be accessed at https://github.com/hyunkim921/cross-field_reconnection. 
  The most significant contributions of this research are a set of figures and 
  results presented in Appendix E-F along with the relevant code in Appendix G. 
  The most crucial aspects of this research can be replicated using the 
  combination of the described code and models in https://github.com/hyunkim921/cross-field_reconnection.

  research investigates the accuracy of oral posture recognition using 
  different feature extraction methods from speech signals in Polish. A 
  total of 32 female and 32 male speakers participated in the study, 
  recording readings from 8 different text samples in two oral postures 
  (with interdental diastema and without). The recorded data was 
  analyzed using 13 widely recognized features, including speech 
  characteristics like pitch, intensity, and formants. The results show 
  that the accuracy of oral posture recognition without additional 
  training is the lowest, at 32% for female speakers and 19% for male 
  speakers. The best accuracy among the features examined was achieved 
  using a combination of spectral and mouth-opening features, reaching 
  63.5% for female speakers and 45.5% for male speakers. This study 
  also found that features related to speech rhythm and jaw position 
  are the most effective in recognizing oral postures, while those 
  related to articulation and mouth position are the least effective. 
  The studied features can be grouped into three categories: 
  articulation-related, jaw-position-related, and breath-related, 
  which differ in accuracy within and across speakers. The best 
  features identified are then combined with machine learning algorithms 
  (LDA, QDA, SVM, RF, and ET) to assess their impact, revealing that 
  Random Forest is the most effective in oral posture recognition from 
  speech signals. The proposed method achieves the highest accuracy, 
  at 70.5% for female speakers and 50% for male speakers, which is 
  significantly better than the baseline (without additional 
  training). The proposed approach is proposed for use in mobile 
  applications that can be trained on a limited dataset. The proposed 
  method is further tested on a larger dataset (with 128 speakers) 
  recorded in natural environments, including conversations, which 
  demonstrates its effectiveness in real-world scenarios. The proposed

  fine-tuning existing computational algorithms to enhance their performance on 
  specific problems. At its core, instruction tuning fine-tunes low-level computer 
  code to maximize efficiency, a practice that has both benefits and drawbacks. 
  Although it lessens the burden on programmers by supplying optimized base 
  code, it also presents a significant challenge due to the intricate relationship 
  between computer instructions and operational functionality. As a result, there 
  is a significant gap in research on this subject, as well as a lack of effective 
  tools that can simplify and automate the process of instruction tuning. To 
  address these limitations, we present iTorch, a novel runtime environment that 
  both automates and simplifies instruction tuning by providing a flexible and 
  extensible framework for doing so. This environment, which is built around 
  autodifferentiation, enables the easy creation of training functions that can 
  efficiently optimize computational algorithms using a variety of optimization 
  techniques. Moreover, iTorch includes multiple runtime features that can both 
  efficiently execute autodifferentiation and provide real-time performance 
  feedback, all while being highly customizable. As a result, we believe that 
  iTorch represents a significant advancement in the field of instruction tuning 
  by making this process easier to do, as well as by providing a more detailed 
  understanding of how computer instructions work. To support our claims, we have 
  conducted a series of experiments using a variety of benchmarks to demonstrate 
  the effectiveness of iTorch in terms of both performance and programming 
  efficiency. Our results show that the code generated by iTorch is not only 
  superior to hand-optimized versions but also has a significant advantage over 
  both the unoptimized and compiler-generated versions of the same code. 
  Furthermore, we have found that the code generated by iTorch achieves the same 
  level of performance as hand-optimized versions, but with a more compact and 
  efficient binary size. As a result, we believe that iTorch has a bright future 
  and is worth continuing to develop and refine, especially in light of the 
  emerging trend of performance-intensive artificial intelligence applications.

method is adapted to use a simplified two-dimensional interface representation in combination with a local grid refinement technique. This modification involves setting a minimum interface thickness of one grid spacing, which acts as a barrier to capture interfaces accurately. A new term is added to the stress tensor to counter the effects of this limit on interface behavior. This approach is applicable to both immiscible and miscible fluid problems. A basic state problem is used to validate the model, showing that the simplified interface representation maintains a stable two-phase state. A temporal integration method is proposed to simulate interface dynamics. A test case involving Rayleigh--Taylor instability is conducted, revealing that the model can capture both short- and long-wavelength wave modes. A significant slowdown is observed in the growth rates of both wave modes when compared to the classical solution. This can be attributed to the dispersion of stress by the model as a result of the two-phase state indicator's blockiness. This effect intensifies as the interface thickness decreases. This research confirms that capturing the effects of monodispersive stress is crucial for improving the accuracy of two-phase flow simulations. This can be achieved by implementing numerical schemes that preserve the positivity of the stress tensor. This approach is efficient for both serial and parallel computing, and it can be coupled with other closure models for both transient and steady-state simulations of two-phase flows. This method's accuracy is demonstrated through a comparison with experimental data on the growth rates of both short- and long-wavelength Rayleigh--Taylor instabilities. This indicates that the model can capture the effects of monodispersive stress on both scales of instability. This research is applied to study the stability of a two-phase flow in a porous medium with a periodic array of constrictions. This induces a short-wavelength instability in the interface, resulting in the detachment of dense droplets. This can be attributed to the high-dispersion stresses generated within the constrictions. This research also reveals that the growth rates of both wave modes are sensitive to the average velocity, with the short-wavelength mode showing a more pronounced sensitivity. This can be related to the effects of continued fragmentation induced by the disspersion of stress. This research is confirmed to be applicable to both primary and secondary fragmentation processes. This indicates that the model can simulate the complex dynamics of particle interaction, including collision and coalescence, as well as jet instability and fragmentation. This research is applied to conduct a numerical experiments on the stability of a two-phase flow in a rotating annulus filled with a random array of obstacles.

However, due to the computational intensity of both importance and bridge sampling, we developed an alternative method that involves integrating out the scale parameter from the generalized gamma distribution and then employing bridge sampling for the remaining distribution.  We evaluated and compared the results obtained from all three methods, incorporating multiple test functions and various prior distributions in our analysis.  Our empirical studies revealed that the proposed bridge sampling algorithm exhibits a significant increase in efficiency when compared to both importance and bridge sampling for the full distribution, while the tests based on the proposed method showed consistent accuracy when compared to the benchmarks obtained from the other methods.  We also discussed the applicability and potential uses of the proposed algorithm.  Additionally, we made both the R and Python code that supports the proposed algorithm freely available on the GitHub platform.  We believe that the proposed bridge sampling algorithm is highly effective and efficient, and we encourage other researchers to utilize and build upon it.  Furthermore, we stress that the proposed algorithm serves as an exemplary application of bridge sampling, and we encourage other researchers to utilize this technique for their own projects.  We also propose the utilization of the proposed algorithm as a base for developing Bayesian methods for testing the symmetry of other distributions.  We further propose the incorporation of the proposed algorithm into Bayesian workflows that involve testing the symmetry of distributions, as well as into tutorials and courses on bridge sampling and Bayesian methods for testing the symmetry of distributions.  We also propose the development of faster bridge sampling algorithms for the proposed application. This standard representation associates each computable function with a corresponding set of directed edges, with the corresponding Turing machine instructions serving as node labels. This labeling method is based on a coding system that maps each Turing machine instruction to a unique combination of natural numbers. As a result, there is a surjective mapping from the natural numbers to these combinations, ensuring that for any set of directed edges there is a corresponding Turing machine that generates the same sequence of natural numbers when given no input. This representation allows us to define a relation (denoted as $\equiv_k$) between two sets of directed edges, indicating that the associated Turing machines produce the same sequence of natural numbers when given up to k inputs. This relation is equivalent to the traditional computable equivalence relation defined using functions. This representation also enables us to define a relation (denoted as $\simeq_k$) between two sets of directed edges, indicating that the associated Turing machines produce the same sequence of natural numbers when given up to k distinct natural numbers. This relation is not computably equivalent to the relation obtained by listing the natural numbers in ascending order and comparing corresponding entries, as demonstrated by an example involving two Turing machines and a specific natural number n. This discrepancy arises because the relation $\simeq_k$ does not imply the ability to determine if two natural numbers are equal when given only their respective lists, as shown through a theoretical discussion and an informal argument using the concept of oracle Turing machines. This example involves a Turing machine that generates an infinite sequence of natural numbers, with the ability to determine if two natural numbers are equal depending on the relation of the associated Turing machines to the oracle. This argument illustrates the connection between the relation $\simeq_k$ and the halting problem, but with an important difference. and labeling data is costly, like needing detailed text transcriptions for 
audio files. To make the most of expensive data labeling, an efficient active 
learning method is crucial. Most active learning methods cater to simple and 
inexpensive data labeling tasks but fall short when transcription-based labeling 
is required. Existing methods often rely on query strategies that select easy 
data points based on their labeling status, neglecting the complexity of the 
transcription task. As a result, they don't effectively prioritize the most 
beneficial data points for human labelers to transcribe. To address this limit 
ation, we present \emph{SRTAL}, a novel active learning method tailored for 
speech recognition task annotations, which prioritizes the most difficult data 
points to transcribe. We achieve this by integrating a automatic speech 
recognition system to generate easy-to-transcribe labels for an initial batch of 
data, thereby establishing a baseline for future comparisons. Additionally, we 
develop a hard data point selection strategy that prioritizes transcriptions 
difficulties. We evaluate \emph{SRTAL} on the Librispeech dataset and the Google 
Speech Dataset. The results show that \emph{SRTAL} significantly outperforms 
baseline AL methods in terms of the accuracy of the trained model, and its 
effectiveness is also demonstrated across various budgets and labeling costs. 
The code for SRTAL will be made publicly available.  \emph{SRTAL} serves as 
a blueprint for developing AL methods for tasks with expensive and complex data 
labeling, such as speech recognition task annotations.  \emph{SRTAL} is superior 
to the current state-of-the-art AL methods in terms of predictive model 
performance, and its source code will be made available to encourage further 
development of AL methods for difficult data labeling tasks. 
\emph{SRTAL} is specifically designed to be scalable and efficient, and its 
technological components are compatible with existing large-scale ASR systems and 
their accelerated training techniques, allowing for large model pre-training 
and few-shot fine-tuning on a subset of the transcription data.

different sampling rates, such as annotations for emotion, tone, or chemical

  Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have commonly used the Backpropagation Through Time algorithm for training, albeit with significant drawbacks. Our research addresses a critical limitation of vanishing gradients in traditional BPTT by introducing an optimized version of Sequential Neural Network, which employs a faster and more efficient learning process. Our proposed method exhibits superior performance, surpassing other alternatives in a benchmark task. Surprisingly, our findings reveal that our optimized sequential model performs better than the fully connected version, even when the hidden state is linearly transformed, which we believe is an unexpected observation requiring further exploration. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/CJ2209564/RNN_BPTT_comparision.
